Use individual-year income data `sample_size_tb` to examine the age distribution, income distributions by year and age, and how closely log income follows a normal distribution.
Use 2020 data for the age-specific analyses and the 2014–2020 data saved in 01 for annual comparisons.
Finally, for individuals aged 26–60 in 2020, calculate the age-class composition of those whose income exceeds each threshold.

## 1 Distributions of individual age and income

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(pins)

# Specify relative paths for the board, figure output directory, and plotting theme.
board <- board_folder("../income_board_replicate")
graph_dir <- "graph"
dir.create(graph_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
source("theme_ipsum_like.R")
theme_set(theme_ipsum())
```

**Loading data and creating age classes**

Load income data `sample_size_tb` from `../income_board_replicate/` and retain observations with positive income `main_var`.
Do not impose additional age, industry, or year restrictions when loading the data.

Calculate individual age `age` as observation year `year` minus the birth year in the first four characters of `birth_date`.
Define `age_class` as `age_20` for ages 20 and under, `age_25` for ages 21–25, and subsequent five-year classes through `age_80` for ages 76–80.
Assign observations above age 80 or with missing age to `age_other`.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

sample_size_tb <- board |> pin_read("sample_size_tb") |> 
  filter(main_var > 0)

size_age_tb <- sample_size_tb |>
  mutate(
    age = as.numeric(year) - as.numeric(str_sub(birth_date, 1, 4)),
    age_class = case_when(
      age <= 20 ~ "age_20",
      age <= 80 ~ str_c("age_", 5 * ceiling(age / 5)),
      TRUE ~ "age_other"
    )
  )

age_class_labels <- c(
  "age_20" = "0–20",
  "age_25" = "21–25", "age_30" = "26–30", "age_35" = "31–35", "age_40" = "36–40",
  "age_45" = "41–45", "age_50" = "46–50", "age_55" = "51–55", "age_60" = "56–60"
)

```

**Age distribution**

Plot a histogram with one-year bins for observations aged 20–100 in 2020.
Apply this age restriction only when creating the figure. In the data generated in 01, observed ages in 2020 range from 20 to 70.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

size_age_tb |> 
  filter(
    year == "2020",
    age >= 20, age <= 100
  ) |> 
ggplot(aes(age)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, 
                 fill = "#2C3E50", color = "white", 
                 linewidth = 0.3) + 
  labs(
    x = "Individual Age (Years)",
    y = "Number of Individuals"
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
ggsave(filename = "age_dist_income.png", path = graph_dir)

```

**Annual comparison of income distributions**

Compare income density curves by year using the positive-income observations selected when loading the data. Impose no additional age restrictions.
Use base-10 logarithmic scales on both axes, with displayed income in yen ranging from $10^3$ to $10^{10}$ and density from $10^{-6}$ to $10^0$.
Because `scale_x_log10()` transforms the horizontal axis before density estimation, the vertical axis shows the density of base-10 log income on a logarithmic scale.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

sample_size_tb |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_density(aes(main_var, color = year)) + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "C") + 
  scale_x_log10() + 
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10^3, 10^{10}), ylim = c(10^{-6}, 10^0)) +
  labs(
    x = "income",
    y = "Density (log scale)",
    color = "Year"
  )
ggsave(filename = "main_var_df_log.png", path = graph_dir)

```

**Income distribution by age**

For observations aged 26–60 in 2020, compare income distributions across seven age classes: 26–30, 31–35, …, 56–60.
As in the annual comparison, estimate the density of base-10 log income and use logarithmic scales on both axes.
Display income in yen from $10^3$ to $10^9$ and density from $10^{-5}$ to $10^0$.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

size_age_tb |> 
  filter(year == "2020",
         age >= 26, age <= 60) |> 
  ggplot() + 
  geom_density(aes(main_var, color = age_class)) + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(
    option = "C", 
    labels = age_class_labels
    ) + 
  scale_x_log10() + 
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(10^3, 10^9), ylim = c(10^{-5}, 10^0)) +
  labs(
    x = "Income (log scale)",
    y = "Density (log scale)", 
    color = "Age Group",
  ) 

ggsave(filename = "main_var_df_age_class_log.png", path = graph_dir)

```

## 2 Comparing log income with a normal distribution: Q-Q plots

Select the seven age classes `age_30`, `age_35`, …, `age_60` (ages 26–60) from the 2020 data.
For each class, take the natural logarithm of income in yen, subtract its median, and divide by the scaled median absolute deviation returned by `mad()` with its default settings.
Do not standardize using the mean and standard deviation.

The standardized value is $z=(\log(Y)-\operatorname{median}(\log(Y)))/\operatorname{MAD}(\log(Y))$, where $Y$ is `main_var`.
Here, MAD is the median absolute deviation from the median multiplied by 1.4826.

Use `stat_qq()` to compare sample quantiles of standardized log income with theoretical quantiles of the standard normal distribution.
Add a reference line with intercept zero and slope one; do not estimate a reference line using `stat_qq_line()`.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

size_age_tb |> 
  filter(year == "2020", 
         age_class %in% c("age_30", "age_35", "age_40",
                          "age_45", "age_50", "age_55", "age_60"), 
         main_var > 0) |> 
  group_by(age_class) |> 
  mutate(log_size = log(main_var), 
         log_size_normalized = (log_size - median(log_size))/mad(log_size) ) |> 
ggplot(aes(sample = log_size_normalized, color = age_class)) + 
  stat_qq(size = 0.7) + #stat_qq_line() + 
  scale_color_viridis_d(
    option = "C", 
    labels = age_class_labels
  ) + 
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color="black") + 
  labs(
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Normalized log(Income)",
    color = "Age Group"
  ) 
ggsave(filename = "income_size_qqplot_by_age.png", path = graph_dir)

```

## 3 Age composition by income threshold

For individuals aged 26–60 in 2020, examine the age composition of those whose income exceeds a threshold.

Set income thresholds `criteria` in yen to $10^{6.6}, 10^{6.8}, \ldots, 10^{10}$, giving 18 points spaced by 0.2 in base-10 logarithms.
First restrict the data to 2020 and ages 26–60, then select observations with `main_var` strictly above each threshold.
Create `frac2_tb` by calculating composition shares `n_ratio`, using the total number selected `n_total` as the denominator and the count in each age class as the numerator.
Omit thresholds with no qualifying observations.

```{r}

# Threshold vector (10^i)
x_val <- 10 ^ seq(6.6, 10, 0.2)

# Use observations aged 26–60 in 2020.
target_tb <- size_age_tb |>
  filter(year == "2020", age >= 26, age <= 60)

frac2_tb <- map_dfr(x_val, function(criteria) {
  sub_tb <- target_tb |> filter(main_var > criteria)

  n_total <- nrow(sub_tb)
  if (n_total == 0) return(NULL)

  sub_tb |>
    count(age_class, name = "n") |>
    transmute(
      age_class,
      n_ratio = n / n_total,
      criteria = criteria,
      n_total = n_total
    )
})

```


**Plotting the shares**

For thresholds with more than 1,000 qualifying individuals (`n_total`), plot age-class shares using points and lines.
The denominator is the total number of individuals aged 26–60 above each threshold, rather than the total population of each age class.
Show the income threshold in yen on a logarithmic horizontal axis and the composition share on the vertical axis, with a displayed range of 0–0.3.

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2

frac2_tb |>
  filter(n_total > 10^3) |>
  ggplot(aes(criteria, n_ratio, color = age_class)) + 
    geom_point() + 
    geom_line() + 
    scale_color_viridis_d(
      option = "C",
      labels = age_class_labels
    ) + 
    scale_x_log10() + 
    labs(
      x = "Income (log scale)",
      y = "Proportion",
      color = "Age Group"
    ) +
    ylim(c(0, .3))
ggsave(filename = "frac2_age_main_var_middile.png", path = graph_dir)

```
